title: Matsushita Electric Industrial Co. v. Zenith Radio Corp.
lead: American television manufacturers allege decades of coordinated predatory pricing; the Court asks whether the record supports an injurious agreement rather than merely concerted conduct.

actors.name: Zenith Radio Corporation
actors.role: American television manufacturer asserting predatory-conspiracy injury.

actors.name: National Union Electric
actors.role: Successor to Emerson, another American claimant.

actors.name: Japanese manufacturers and American affiliates
actors.role: Defendants alleged to have funded American losses with Japanese profits; twenty-one petitioned for review.

proceedings: The consolidated district court excluded substantial evidence and entered summary judgment for defendants.
The Third Circuit restored evidence and reversed the pertinent summary judgment.
The Supreme Court reversed and remanded for consideration of sufficiently unambiguous additional evidence, otherwise reinstatement of summary judgment.
limits: The conspiracy was alleged, not found. Admissibility rulings, the separate Antidumping Act decision, and sovereign compulsion remained outside the Court’s decision. The remand was qualified rather than unconditional final judgment on every claim.

review.basis: Individually written and compared with the canonical full brief; no new independent opinion audit claimed.

sections.title: Two American businesses allege a long plan to monopolize television sales
sections.cue: What sequence of losses and later gains did their theory require?
paragraphs: Zenith manufactured and sold televisions in the United States. National Union Electric succeeded Emerson Radio, which stopped television manufacture in 1970 after substantial losses. They alleged that Japanese manufacturers and American affiliates kept Japanese prices artificially high to fund below-cost American sales, eliminate American competitors, then raise prices here to recover losses through monopoly profits. These were allegations, not Supreme Court findings of a historical scheme.

National Union Electric sued in New Jersey in 1970, using an alleged 1960 start; Zenith sued in Pennsylvania in 1974, alleging a 1953 start. The cases consolidated in the Eastern District of Pennsylvania in 1974. Claims invoked the Sherman, Robinson-Patman, and Wilson Tariff Acts alongside a separately adjudicated Antidumping Act theory. Twenty-one petitioners remained after the Third Circuit sustained judgment for three original defendants.

sources.pinpoint: Alleged scheme and procedure; 475 U.S. 577–580 & nn.1–4, 591 n.13

sections.title: Years of discovery end in summary judgment, then appellate restoration
sections.cue: Which evidence and issues reached the Supreme Court?
paragraphs: The district court required final pretrial statements identifying documentary evidence with preclusive effect. It excluded much governmental, business, and expert material, then assessed admissible evidence by category and together. Some agreements would not hurt these competitors, and low prices more plausibly reflected competition. It entered summary judgment, including dependent monopolization and discrimination claims.

The Third Circuit restored substantial evidence and reversed. It saw possible coordination in a concentrated Japanese market with entry barriers, high fixed costs and excess capacity, export minimum or check prices arranged with Japan’s Ministry of International Trade and Industry, a five-company limit on each producer’s American distributors, and concealed rebates undermining those check prices. Together these might support the alleged scheme.

Supreme Court review excluded admissibility rulings. The Court also declined the separate Antidumping Act issue because the petition and argument did not properly present it. The forty-volume party appendix was an evidentiary record, not an appendix to the published judicial opinion. Justice Powell wrote the five-Justice majority.

sources.pinpoint: Procedure; Court and result; 475 U.S. 576–582 & nn.2–5

sections.title: Powell asks whether agreements caused the kind of injury claimed
sections.cue: Why were price-raising arrangements insufficient by themselves?
paragraphs: Antitrust injury required more than showing some concerted conduct. Cartel conditions confined to Japan did not alone establish these American losses, though foreign conduct affecting American commerce could fall within the Sherman Act. The plaintiffs needed a connection to American predatory pricing.

American price floors and distribution restrictions could raise prices or limit output, potentially benefiting competing American producers even if independently unlawful. Describing them as one overarching conspiracy did not remove the requirement of injury antitrust law recognizes. The low-price campaign supplied the potentially harmful theory.

The Court did not adopt a universal cost test or decide whether pricing above an incremental-cost measure could ever support recovery. Defendants had not challenged the Third Circuit’s per se characterization of a proved predatory agreement. The case instead concerned evidentiary support for this horizontal conspiracy and resulting injury.

sections.title: Economic context limits reasonable conspiracy inferences
sections.cue: What made the alleged long campaign implausible to the majority?
paragraphs: Under Rule 56, once the movant satisfies its burden, an opponent needs specific facts permitting a rational favorable verdict, not speculative doubt. The initial burden had already been resolved below. Reasonable inferences still favored the opponent, but antitrust substance constrained them: behavior equally consistent with independent competition and conspiracy did not alone establish unlawful agreement. Evidence had to tend to exclude independent action. A theory contrary to economic incentives needed more persuasive support.

Predation entails current losses for uncertain future recoupment. It requires eliminating rivals, creating monopoly power, preventing new entry, and maintaining high prices long enough to repay accumulated losses and earn returns. Multiple conspirators also must allocate losses and future profits while resisting free riding and cheating. Enough ordinary-price sales could keep targets alive.

The alleged campaign lasted roughly two decades without success. RCA and Zenith still held the two largest individual retail shares, together near forty percent, while Japanese firms collectively approached fifty percent. The effort supposedly continued against Zenith, with no demonstrated barriers ensuring durable monopoly prices. Greater share through losing sales also enlarged the loss needing recoupment.

Japanese profits and unused capacity suggested ability to finance exports, not a reason for unrecoverable losses. Erroneous conspiracy inferences could chill the discounts antitrust protects. Failed predatory cartels burdened their members; successful recoupment cartels themselves remained unlawful and detectable. Price floors, distribution limits, and Japanese agreements therefore suggested price raising or ordinary competition rather than this extended loss-making design. The majority also accepted criticism of expert below-cost calculations based on constructed assumptions instead of actual cost data, despite restored admissibility. A plausible motive alone would still not make equally consistent conduct enough.

sections.title: White regards the competing explanations as trial arguments
sections.cue: Why did the dissent think the majority weighed evidence?
paragraphs: Justice White, joined by Brennan, Blackmun, and Stevens, accepted the rational-factfinder standard and favorable inferences but disputed implementation. Comparing conspiracy’s plausibility with independent action could become judicial weighing rather than identifying a permissible favorable inference. Prior insufficiency cases did not authorize a trial-like balance of all proof.

Economist DePodwin explained how restricting Japanese demand increased American exports and depressed prices, and how suppressing rivalry among Japanese firms enabled coordinated attacks on American customers. White saw that as a factual issue rather than something displaced by the majority’s preferred model. The Third Circuit had linked arrangements and identified evidence of long-term below-cost sales, not simply assumed every agreement caused injury.

Whether firms prioritized growth and whether expert methods were reliable belonged to the factfinder on this record. White would affirm and remand for trial, likewise leaving sovereign compulsion undecided.

sections.title: The qualified remand permits a final search for stronger evidence
sections.cue: What did the Supreme Court actually order?
paragraphs: On March 26, 1986, the Court reversed the Third Circuit and remanded. That court could consider other sufficiently unambiguous evidence of the alleged predatory scheme; without it, defendants were entitled to reinstated summary judgment. Powell was joined by Burger, Marshall, Rehnquist, and O’Connor, producing five votes to four.

Sovereign compulsion remained undecided because the claimed government requirement concerned minimum prices, while potential injury arose from distinct low-price conduct. The Court also left admissibility and the separate Antidumping Act ruling outside review. It made no trial finding about every transaction and no universal factual rule about low prices. The assigned summary compresses the two plaintiffs and conditional disposition, which the full brief restores.

sources.pinpoint: Court and result; Remand and limits; 475 U.S. 597–598
